body.summary: PSI cannot yet say how a fabric or a plastic burns in this cabin. The studies of solid materials stayed at or below normal air, and the tests that did reach 34% oxygen burned gas or liquid fuel.

points.text: BASS-II, the main study of solid materials, only ever lowered the oxygen. It never went above cabin air.
points.quote: Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration (oxygen varied below 21% by adding nitrogen).

points.text: BRE is the strongest lead. It used a gas burner built to imitate burning solids, and it tested this exact atmosphere.
In BRE, turning off the airflow did not put the flame out once oxygen was raised. Stopping ventilation is a standard first response to a fire on a spacecraft.
points.quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft

points.text: FLEX mapped where droplet flames go out as oxygen and pressure change, with tests up to 34% oxygen at reduced pressure.
points.quote: determine the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) as a function of ambient pressure

body.caution: All of this was measured in weightlessness. Nothing in PSI was measured at lunar gravity.

body.summary: Liquid-fuel tests cover this atmosphere well. Solid materials do not: the nearest test of a solid is still at ordinary cabin air.

points.text: FLEX burned droplets right around this oxygen level and pressure, with and without a suppressant gas.
points.quote: measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6

points.text: BRE names this atmosphere as one of the three it set out to test.
In a small cabin, detecting a fire early matters most. SAME measured what smoke looks like to a detector in weightlessness.
points.quote: SAME will provide quantitative data on the sensitivity of these detectors to reduced gravity smokes

body.caution: A rover on the Moon sits in one-sixth gravity, which no test here reproduces.

body.summary: This is the best-covered case in the archive. Solids, liquids and gases were all burned at or near cabin air, inside real station hardware.

points.text: BASS-II burned rods, slabs, films and fabric at cabin oxygen and below, to find where each one stops burning.
points.quote: Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

points.text: Saffire lit samples up to a metre long inside an uncrewed cargo ship. These are the only large fires in the set.
points.quote: determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity

points.text: The working assumption behind these studies is that, given airflow, a material burns at least as well in orbit as on the ground.
points.quote: materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity

body.caution: Several of these tables do not list pressure. Cabin pressure is used for them, and those marks are drawn hollow.

body.summary: Nothing in the archive comes close to pure oxygen. The highest oxygen level tested in a surrounding atmosphere is about 40%.

points.text: The 85% oxygen values in CFI-G are not a pure-oxygen atmosphere. They are a stream of oxygen injected into fuel gas.
points.quote: an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame

points.text: NASA screens spacecraft materials at normal gravity, which is why orbital studies such as BASS exist.
points.quote: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.

body.caution: For a suit, treat this archive as background physics, not as evidence about suit materials.
